name: Western Huasteca Nahuatl
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 3.2. Two degrees of stress are clearly distinguishable: (1) primary stress, manifested by increased loudness of the syllable, together with a marked rise in pitch, and (2) secondary stress, less loud than primary stress, and accompanied by little or no rise in pitch. A few monosyllabic words always have primary stress. Polysyllabic words (i.e. words of two or more syllables) show primary stress on the penult. Words of three or more syllables show in addition secondary stress on the first syllable in phrase initial, and in phrase medial when preceded by a polysyllable. Preceded by a monosyllable, a polysyllable shows only primary stress on the penult; secondary stress falls on the monosyllable, provided it is not one of those bearing primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Croft, Kenneth. 1951. Practical orthography for Matlapa Nahuatl. International Journal of American Linguistics 17(1): 32-36.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.2 'Nahuatl prosodics', p. 33 (archive.org issue PDF p. 35); loanword note sec. 6, p. 35

Preceded by a monosyllable, a polysyllable shows only primary stress on the penult; secondary stress falls on the monosyllable, provided it is not one of those bearing primary stress.'), fol…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word (primary stress = loudness plus pitch rise); a small set of monosyllables carry inherent primary stress; Spanish loans largely conform, with deviant stress marked in transcription.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Words of three or more syllables take a secondary stress (loudness without pitch rise) on the first syllable when phrase-initial or when preceded by a polysyllable; after a monosyllable the secondary stress falls on that monosyllable instead (unless it is an inherently primary-stressed monosyllable).
new_statements.exceptions: A few monosyllables always bear primary stress; sec. 6 (p. 35): 'a large number of Spanish loans follow the Nahuatl stress pattern (see 3.2); thus in transcribing texts the present writer has adopted the practice of marking stress only where it deviates from the usual pattern' (e.g. mexor 'better' keeps final stress). Beller & Beller 1979: 205 likewise 'except for a few rare exceptions', written with an accent when they occur.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress (penult of the word); secondary stress placement is stated relative to the phonological phrase (phrase-initial vs. after mono-/polysyllables); phrases delimited by pauses with phrase-final glottal stop (sec. 3.3). Corroborated for Huasteca Nahuatl generally by Beller & Beller 1979: 205 ('Stress is on the penultimate syllable except for a few rare exceptions') and Beller & Cowan de Beller Curso vol. 1 p. 11 ('El acento prosodico... recae sobre la penultima silaba aunque esta termine en consonante').
new_statements.identity_note: Primary statement (Croft 1951) describes the Nahuatl of Matlapa, San Luis Potosi (one informant, Arcadio Sagahon), which lies in the Western Huasteca (nhw, west2624) area; Beller & Beller 1979 explicitly identify Croft's Matlapa work as describing their 'W dialect'. The corroborating Beller & Beller 1979 sketch ('Huasteca Nahuatl') pools both Huasteca dialects: principal consultant from Cuatenahuatl near Huautla, Hidalgo (their Eastern dialect = east2538/nhe), Western examples from Tamazunchale, SLP; its penultimate-stress statement is given for Huasteca Nahuatl as a whole without W/E qualification. The Beller & Cowan de Beller Curso (vol. 1 p. 11, same rule in Spanish) is mainly Huautla (Eastern) speech.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2 p. 33: two degrees of stress; a few monosyllables always bear primary stress; polysyllables have primary stress on the penult; words of 3+ syllables add secondary stress on the first syllable (phrase-initial, or phrase-medial after a polysyllable). Sec. 6 p. 35: most Spanish loans follow the Nahuatl pattern; stress marked only where it deviates.
